questiontext.text:
{@E[1]@} Let \(x\) be the number of {@E[2]@} and \(y\) the number of {@E[3]@}. Write an inequality for each condition.

(a) {@E[10]@}

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) {@E[11]@}

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

(c) {@E[12]@}

[[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
(a) The cost, or the amount used, is \({@p1@}x + {@p2@}y\), and ‘at most’ gives \(\le\): \({@ta1@}\). Dividing by \({@g1@}\) gives the simpler form \({@ta1s@}\).

(b) The total number is \(x + y\), and ‘at most’ gives \({@ta2@}\).

(c) \({@ta3@}\). The words decide the sign: at least \(\ge\), more than \(\gt\), fewer than \(\lt\), at most \(\le\). For ‘times as many’, check with numbers before you write the inequality.

Each limit on what is possible becomes one inequality. Any equivalent form, such as both sides multiplied by the same positive number, is accepted.

questiondescription.text:
Linear Programming: writing constraints from words

Grade 12 CBE Core 1.4 (a) / Essential 1.4 (a): Write a budget, a total and a third condition (at least, more than, fewer than, or k times as many) as linear inequalities in x and y.

Core and Essential

This question is adapted from Chapter 8, Exercise A, question 7 of School Mathematics Project, SMP Book 5 (Metric), ed. P. G. Bowie, Cambridge University Press, 1969: sentences of conditions turned into inequalities, extended to two-unknown budgets and capacities, with Kenyan contexts, new numbers and named feedback.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core and Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

feedbackvariables.text: c1: lcls(ans1, ta1); s1: lcls(ans1, sw1);

node.description: Same region as the budget inequality

truefeedback.text: Your inequality says the total is {@E[19]@} or more. ‘At most’ means the total cannot go above {@E[19]@}.
You matched the numbers to the wrong letters: your inequality puts \({@p2@}\) with \(x\), but \(x\) counts the {@E[2]@}.
Your inequality does not allow a total of exactly {@E[19]@}. ‘At most’ includes the limit itself.

falsefeedback.text: Multiply the amount for one of the {@E[2]@} by \(x\) and the amount for one of the {@E[3]@} by \(y\), add, and compare the total with the limit in the sentence.

feedbackvariables.text: c2: lcls(ans2, ta2); s2: is(lcls(ans2, one2x) = "same" or lcls(ans2, one2y) = "same");

truefeedback.text: Your inequality says the total number is \({@NN@}\) or more. ‘At most \({@NN@}\)’ means it cannot go above \({@NN@}\).
Your inequality limits one kind only. The sentence limits the two kinds together.
Your inequality does not allow exactly \({@NN@}\) altogether. ‘At most \({@NN@}\)’ includes \({@NN@}\) itself.

falsefeedback.text: The sentence is about the two kinds together: write their total in letters, then compare it with \({@NN@}\).

feedbackvariables.text: c3: lcls(ans3, ta3); s3: lcls(ans3, e3);

falsefeedback.text: Translate the words with the table: at least \(\ge\), more than \(\gt\), fewer than \(\lt\). Check which letter the sentence is about.
